a: the city of Samaria
p: The oldest copies say Philip went to "the" city of Samaria; most later ones, and the Tyndale House edition, say "a" city.

readings.w: P74 (600s), Codex Sinaiticus and Vaticanus (300s), Alexandrinus (400s) and a few others (reported by Metzger); NA28 (in brackets), SBLGNT, Westcott-Hort
readings.orig: εἰς τὴν πόλιν τῆς Σαμαρείας
readings.en: to the city of Samaria
readings.plain: the city of Samaria

readings.w: Ephraemi (C, 400s), Bezae (D, 400s), Laudianus (E, 500s) and most later manuscripts; Tyndale House GNT, Tregelles, Byzantine text, Textus Receptus
readings.orig: εἰς πόλιν τῆς Σαμαρείας
readings.en: to a city of Samaria
readings.plain: a city of Samaria

why: The article has the oldest support, and a scribe who could not tell which city was meant had a reason to drop it, so the Plain follows NA28 and the SBLGNT. NA28 prints it in brackets because the committee was not sure, and the Tyndale House edition (THGNT), like Tregelles before it, judged the article secondary and prints "a city."
b: With "the," Luke probably means the region's main city, old Samaria, which Herod the Great had rebuilt as Sebaste. Without it, any town will do, and some have suggested Sychar, or Gitta, Simon's home town in later tradition. The KJV says "the city of Samaria" even though its Greek has no article.

a: "This man is the Power of God," they said, "the one called Great."
t: "The Power called Great" or "the great power"?
p: The older text has a title: the Power of God "that is called Great." The Byzantine text drops "called."

readings.w: Nearly all early manuscripts, among them Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus and Vaticanus; NA28, SBLGNT, THGNT
readings.orig: ἡ δύναμις τοῦ θεοῦ ἡ καλουμένη Μεγάλη
readings.en: the power of God that is called Great
readings.plain: "This man is the Power of God," they said, "the one called Great."

readings.w: Byzantine text, Textus Receptus (KJV "This man is the great power of God")
readings.orig: ἡ δύναμις τοῦ θεοῦ ἡ μεγάλη
readings.en: the great power of God
readings.plain: "This man is the great power of God," they said.

why: "Called" is in the oldest copies. It makes "Great Power" a known title, which is the harder and more interesting reading; dropping one word turned it into plain praise.
b: "The Great Power" looks like a name for a divine being, and some scholars think the Samaritans used it of their high God. See the note on this verse.

a: the Spirit was given
p: Two of the oldest copies say only "the Spirit"; most others, and the Tyndale House edition, say "the Holy Spirit."

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus and Vaticanus (300s) with a few others (reported by Metzger); NA28, SBLGNT, Westcott-Hort
readings.orig: δίδοται τὸ πνεῦμα
readings.en: the Spirit is given
readings.plain: the Spirit was given

readings.w: Most other manuscripts (reported by Metzger); Tyndale House GNT, Tregelles, Byzantine text, Textus Receptus (KJV "the Holy Ghost was given")
readings.orig: δίδοται τὸ πνεῦμα τὸ ἅγιον
readings.en: the Holy Spirit is given
readings.plain: the Holy Spirit was given

why: Copyists far more often added "Holy" to "the Spirit" than took it away, since "Holy Spirit" stands in 8:15, 17 and 19. The shorter reading is followed, though the Tyndale House editors judged the other way. The sense does not change.

a: plead with the Lord
p: The KJV's "pray God" follows the later text; the older copies have "the Lord."

readings.w: The oldest manuscripts; NA28, SBLGNT, THGNT
readings.orig: δεήθητι τοῦ κυρίου
readings.en: pray to the Lord
readings.plain: plead with the Lord

readings.w: Byzantine text, Textus Receptus (KJV "pray God")
readings.orig: δεήθητι τοῦ θεοῦ
readings.en: pray to God
readings.plain: plead with God

why: "The Lord" has the earlier support and matches Simon's reply in 8:24, which asks them to pray "to the Lord."

a: [The oldest manuscripts do not have this verse.]
p: The KJV's verse 37, "I believe that Jesus Christ is the Son of God," is not in the oldest manuscripts.

readings.w: P45 (200s), P74 (600s), Codex Sinaiticus and Vaticanus (300s), Alexandrinus (400s), Ephraemi (400s), the Byzantine majority, the Syriac Peshitta and the Coptic (reported by Metzger); NA28, SBLGNT, THGNT, Robinson-Pierpont
readings.orig: (the verse is absent)
readings.en: (no verse 37)
readings.plain: [The oldest manuscripts do not have this verse.]

readings.w: Codex Laudianus (E, 500s), a few later minuscules (among them 323, 945 and 1739), many Old Latin manuscripts and some copies of the Latin Vulgate; known to Irenaeus (about AD 180, Against Heresies 3.12.8) and Cyprian (about 250); Textus Receptus (KJV)
readings.orig: εἶπε δὲ ὁ Φίλιππος· εἰ πιστεύεις ἐξ ὅλης τῆς καρδίας, ἔξεστιν. ἀποκριθεὶς δὲ εἶπε· πιστεύω τὸν υἱὸν τοῦ θεοῦ εἶναι τὸν Ἰησοῦν Χριστόν.
readings.en: Philip said, "If you believe with all your heart, you may." He answered, "I believe that Jesus Christ is the Son of God."
readings.plain: Philip said, "If you believe with your whole heart, you may." He answered, "I believe that Jesus Christ is the Son of God."

why: The verse is missing from every early Greek manuscript and from the great majority of later ones, the Byzantine text included. If it had been there from the start, no one had a reason to cut it. It reads like a baptismal question and answer that a scribe wrote in the margin, because it seemed wrong for the eunuch to be baptized with no confession of faith; from the margin it slipped into the text.
b: The words are old: Irenaeus quotes the eunuch's confession about AD 180, so the addition was in circulation in the 100s, probably in the Western text. Erasmus did not find it in the main manuscript he used for his Greek New Testament of 1516; according to Metzger he took it from the margin of another manuscript, thinking scribes had left it out by mistake. From Erasmus it passed into the Textus Receptus and the KJV. Modern Bibles print it in a footnote and keep the number 37 empty, so that verse numbers still match. See the note on this verse.

a: the Lord's Spirit snatched Philip away
t: The Spirit falls on the eunuch (a Western reading)
p: A few witnesses say the Holy Spirit fell on the eunuch and an angel carried Philip off.

readings.w: Nearly all Greek manuscripts; NA28, SBLGNT, THGNT, Byzantine text, Textus Receptus
readings.orig: πνεῦμα κυρίου ἥρπασεν τὸν Φίλιππον
readings.en: the Spirit of the Lord snatched Philip
readings.plain: the Lord's Spirit snatched Philip away

readings.w: A corrector of Codex Alexandrinus, a few later minuscules, and some Old Latin, Vulgate and Syriac witnesses (reported by Metzger)
readings.orig: πνεῦμα ἅγιον ἐπέπεσεν ἐπὶ τὸν εὐνοῦχον, ἄγγελος δὲ κυρίου ἥρπασεν τὸν Φίλιππον
readings.en: the Holy Spirit fell on the eunuch, and an angel of the Lord snatched Philip
readings.plain: the Holy Spirit fell on the eunuch, and an angel of the Lord snatched Philip away

why: The longer reading has thin support and looks like a deliberate improvement: it makes sure the eunuch receives the Spirit, as the Samaritans did (8:17), and it brings back the angel of 8:26. The usual text is shorter and harder to explain as a change.
b: Codex Bezae, the chief Greek witness to the Western text of Acts, has lost its pages for 8:29–10:14, so for these chapters the Western readings come from other copies and the early translations.

a: He replied
p: The KJV reads "And the Lord said"; the oldest manuscripts have only "and he."

readings.w: The oldest manuscripts; NA28, SBLGNT, THGNT
readings.orig: ὁ δέ
readings.en: and he [said]
readings.plain: He replied

readings.w: Byzantine text, Textus Receptus (KJV "And the Lord said")
readings.orig: Ὁ δὲ κύριος εἶπεν
readings.en: and the Lord said
readings.plain: The Lord replied

why: The short Greek "and he" leaves the verb "said" to be understood, a common Greek way of telling a dialogue. Scribes filled it out with "the Lord said," which also makes plain who is speaking. The shorter wording is older and the kind a scribe would expand.

a: whom you are persecuting.
p: The KJV adds "it is hard for thee to kick against the pricks" here. In the Greek manuscripts the saying belongs to 26:14.

readings.w: All early Greek manuscripts and almost all later ones; NA28, SBLGNT, THGNT, Byzantine text
readings.orig: Ἐγώ εἰμι Ἰησοῦς ὃν σὺ διώκεις·
readings.en: I am Jesus, whom you are persecuting
readings.plain: whom you are persecuting.

readings.w: Some Latin manuscripts (Old Latin and Vulgate copies), from which Erasmus put the words into his Greek text; Textus Receptus (KJV)
readings.orig: ὃν σὺ διώκεις· σκληρόν σοι πρὸς κέντρα λακτίζειν
readings.en: whom you are persecuting; kicking against the goads is hard on you
readings.plain: whom you are persecuting. Kicking against the goads is hard on you.

why: The words are in the Greek of 26:14, where Paul retells the story. Here they come from Latin copies that filled out chapter 9 from chapter 26. Erasmus translated them from the Latin into Greek for his edition (Metzger), so the Textus Receptus has words at 9:5–6 that almost no Greek manuscript has there. This entry and the next go together.
b: The goads were the pointed sticks used to drive oxen; for the saying itself, see 26:14.

a: But get up and go into the city.
p: The KJV's "And he trembling and astonished said, Lord, what wilt thou have me to do?" goes with the addition in 9:5.

readings.w: All early Greek manuscripts and almost all later ones; NA28, SBLGNT, THGNT, Byzantine text
readings.orig: ἀλλὰ ἀνάστηθι καὶ εἴσελθε εἰς τὴν πόλιν
readings.en: but get up and enter the city
readings.plain: But get up and go into the city.

readings.w: Some Latin manuscripts, translated into Greek by Erasmus; Textus Receptus (KJV)
readings.orig: τρέμων τε καὶ θαμβῶν εἶπε· κύριε, τί με θέλεις ποιῆσαι; καὶ ὁ κύριος πρὸς αὐτόν· ἀνάστηθι καὶ εἴσελθε εἰς τὴν πόλιν
readings.en: trembling and astonished he said, Lord, what do you want me to do? And the Lord said to him, Get up and enter the city
readings.plain: " Trembling and astonished, Saul said, "Lord, what do you want me to do?" The Lord told him, "Get up and go into the city.

why: Like the goads saying in 9:5, these words were drawn from Paul's later retelling ("What shall I do, Lord?" 22:10) into Latin copies of chapter 9, and Erasmus put them into Greek; Metzger reports no Greek manuscript with them here. This entry and the one on 9:5 go together.

a: he saw nothing
p: The modern editions read that Saul saw "nothing"; the Byzantine text, followed by the KJV, has "no one."

readings.w: SBLGNT, THGNT, Westcott-Hort, Tregelles, NA27
readings.orig: οὐδὲν ἔβλεπεν
readings.en: he saw nothing
readings.plain: he saw nothing

readings.w: Byzantine text, Textus Receptus (KJV "he saw no man")
readings.orig: οὐδένα ἔβλεπεν
readings.en: he saw no one
readings.plain: he saw no one

why: "Nothing" says plainly that Saul was blind, which is the point of 9:9. "No one" may have come in from 9:7, where the companions "saw no one." The two words differ by one letter.
b: NA28 did not revise the text of Acts (only the Catholic Letters were changed from NA27), so it should read "nothing" with NA27. The Tyndale House word data used on this site list NA28 with "no one," which may be a slip in the data; until that is settled this entry does not count NA28 on either side.

a: a man in a vision
t: "In a vision": in some manuscripts only
p: Some of the oldest copies do not say that Saul saw Ananias "in a vision"; NA28 prints the words in brackets.

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s) and most later manuscripts; SBLGNT, Westcott-Hort, NA28 (in brackets), Byzantine text, Textus Receptus
readings.orig: ἄνδρα ἐν ὁράματι
readings.en: a man in a vision
readings.plain: a man in a vision

readings.w: P74 (600s), Codex Sinaiticus (300s), Alexandrinus (400s) and others (reported by Metzger)
readings.orig: ἄνδρα
readings.en: a man
readings.plain: a man

why: The words may be a scribe's explanation, since Saul was blind and could only "see" Ananias in a vision; that they stand in different places in different manuscripts points the same way. But they are in Vaticanus and most copies, so the editors kept them in brackets (Metzger), and the Plain keeps them. The meaning is the same either way: 9:10 has already said that the Lord spoke "in a vision."

a: proclaiming Jesus
p: The older text says Saul proclaimed "Jesus"; the later text and the KJV say "Christ."

readings.w: The oldest manuscripts; NA28, SBLGNT, THGNT
readings.orig: ἐκήρυσσεν τὸν Ἰησοῦν
readings.en: he proclaimed Jesus
readings.plain: proclaiming Jesus

readings.w: Byzantine text, Textus Receptus (KJV "he preached Christ")
readings.orig: ἐκήρυσσεν τὸν χριστόν
readings.en: he proclaimed the Christ
readings.plain: proclaiming the Messiah

why: "Jesus" has the early support. In Acts the claim is about a person: this Jesus, whom Saul had persecuted, is the Son of God. The later reading makes the sentence say that the Messiah is the Son of God, a claim about a title.

a: His disciples
p: The oldest copies say Saul's own "disciples" let him down; most later ones say "the disciples."

readings.w: P74, Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus, Vaticanus and Ephraemi (reported by Metzger); NA28, SBLGNT, THGNT
readings.orig: οἱ μαθηταὶ αὐτοῦ
readings.en: his disciples
readings.plain: His disciples

readings.w: Byzantine text, Textus Receptus (KJV "the disciples")
readings.orig: αὐτὸν οἱ μαθηταί
readings.en: the disciples took him
readings.plain: The disciples

why: "His disciples" is the reading of the oldest manuscripts and the harder one: it is strange that a new believer already has followers, so scribes changed it. Some scholars think the original was "they took him" and that the pronoun slipped in by accident; most editors accept "his disciples," meaning people Saul had brought to faith in Damascus.

a: in the Lord's name
t: "The Lord" or "the Lord Jesus"? And where verse 29 begins
p: The Byzantine text and the KJV read "the Lord Jesus." Modern Greek editions, and many modern Bibles, put this clause at the end of 9:28.

readings.w: The oldest manuscripts; NA28, SBLGNT, THGNT
readings.orig: ἐν τῷ ὀνόματι τοῦ κυρίου
readings.en: in the name of the Lord
readings.plain: in the Lord's name

readings.w: Byzantine text, Textus Receptus (KJV)
readings.orig: ἐν τῷ ὀνόματι τοῦ κυρίου Ἰησοῦ
readings.en: in the name of the Lord Jesus
readings.plain: in the name of the Lord Jesus

why: "Jesus" is a natural addition after "the Lord"; the shorter text is older, so the Plain follows it. The verse break is a different matter. This site numbers every verse as the KJV does, and the KJV starts 9:29 with this clause, so the Plain does too. NA28 and the SBLGNT print it as the end of 9:28. Verse numbers were added in the 1500s and are in no manuscript.
b: If your Bible follows the Greek editions' numbering, you will find "speaking boldly in the name of the Lord" at the end of 9:28. The words are the same; only the number differs.

a: the church was at peace. It was being built up and kept moving forward in the fear of the Lord, and with the Holy Spirit's encouragement it grew larger and larger
p: The oldest copies speak of one "church" across Judea, Galilee and Samaria; the later text and the KJV say "the churches."

readings.w: P74, Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus, Vaticanus, Ephraemi and others (reported by Metzger); NA28, SBLGNT, THGNT
readings.orig: Ἡ μὲν οὖν ἐκκλησία ... εἶχεν εἰρήνην οἰκοδομουμένη ... ἐπληθύνετο
readings.en: the church had peace, being built up ... it was multiplied
readings.plain: the church was at peace. It was being built up and kept moving forward in the fear of the Lord, and with the Holy Spirit's encouragement it grew larger and larger

readings.w: Laudianus (E, 500s) and most later manuscripts; Byzantine text, Textus Receptus (KJV "Then had the churches rest")
readings.orig: Αἱ μὲν οὖν ἐκκλησίαι ... εἶχον εἰρήνην οἰκοδομούμεναι ... ἐπληθύνοντο
readings.en: the churches had peace, being built up ... they were multiplied
readings.plain: the churches were at peace. They were being built up and kept moving forward in the fear of the Lord, and with the Holy Spirit's encouragement they grew larger and larger

why: The singular has much the stronger early support. Scribes used to Paul's "the churches of Judea" (Galatians 1:22) and to Acts 15:41 and 16:5 made it plural. The singular matters: this is the first place where "church" means believers spread over a whole region, not one gathering in one city.

a: a tanner who has a house by the sea."
t: "He will tell you what you must do"
p: The KJV's "he shall tell thee what thou oughtest to do" is in very few manuscripts.

readings.w: All early manuscripts and the Byzantine majority; NA28, SBLGNT, THGNT, Robinson-Pierpont
readings.orig: ᾧ ἐστιν οἰκία παρὰ θάλασσαν
readings.en: whose house is by the sea
readings.plain: a tanner who has a house by the sea."

readings.w: A handful of late manuscripts and some copies of the Latin Vulgate; Textus Receptus (KJV)
readings.orig: ... παρὰ θάλασσαν· οὗτος λαλήσει σοι τί σε δεῖ ποιεῖν
readings.en: ... by the sea; he will tell you what you must do
readings.plain: a tanner who has a house by the sea. He will tell you what you must do."

why: The words are borrowed from 9:6 and 11:14 and are missing from nearly every Greek manuscript, the Byzantine majority included. They came into the printed Greek text through Erasmus' editions.

a: coming down, like a great linen sheet let down by its four corners to the ground
p: Later manuscripts say the sheet came down "to him," "tied at the four corners."

readings.w: NA28, SBLGNT, Westcott-Hort, from the oldest manuscripts
readings.orig: καταβαῖνον σκεῦός τι ὡς ὀθόνην μεγάλην τέσσαρσιν ἀρχαῖς καθιέμενον ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς
readings.en: descending, some vessel like a great sheet, by four corners let down on the earth
readings.plain: coming down, like a great linen sheet let down by its four corners to the ground

readings.w: Tyndale House GNT
readings.orig: ... τέσσαρσιν ἀρχαῖς δεδεμένον καὶ καθιέμενον ...
readings.en: ... tied by four corners and let down ...
readings.plain: coming down, like a great linen sheet tied at its four corners and let down to the ground

readings.w: Byzantine text, Textus Receptus (KJV "descending unto him ... knit at the four corners, and let down")
readings.orig: καταβαῖνον ἐπ’ αὐτὸν ... τέσσαρσιν ἀρχαῖς δεδεμένον καὶ καθιέμενον ...
readings.en: descending upon him ... tied by four corners and let down ...
readings.plain: coming down to him, like a great linen sheet tied at its four corners and let down to the ground

why: The shortest form is the hardest to explain as a change, and the extra words look like a scribe's attempt to picture how a sheet could be lowered by its corners. The Tyndale House editors, though, judged "tied" original and its loss an accident. The picture is the same in every reading.

a: all the four-footed animals and creeping things of the earth and birds of the sky
p: The later text adds "wild animals" to the list, as the KJV does.

readings.w: The oldest manuscripts; NA28, SBLGNT, THGNT
readings.orig: πάντα τὰ τετράποδα καὶ ἑρπετὰ τῆς γῆς καὶ πετεινὰ τοῦ οὐρανοῦ
readings.en: all the four-footed animals and reptiles of the earth and birds of the sky
readings.plain: all the four-footed animals and creeping things of the earth and birds of the sky

readings.w: Byzantine text, Textus Receptus (KJV "all manner of fourfooted beasts of the earth, and wild beasts, and creeping things, and fowls of the air")
readings.orig: πάντα τὰ τετράποδα τῆς γῆς καὶ τὰ θηρία καὶ τὰ ἑρπετὰ καὶ τὰ πετεινὰ τοῦ οὐρανοῦ
readings.en: all the four-footed animals of the earth and the wild animals and the reptiles and the birds of the sky
readings.plain: all the four-footed animals of the earth, the wild animals, the creeping things and the birds of the sky

why: "Wild animals" was probably brought in from Peter's retelling in 11:6, where it belongs. The shorter list echoes the three kinds of animals of Genesis 6:20.

a: three men are searching for you
t: Three men, two men, or just "men"?
p: Most early copies say "three men"; Vaticanus says "two"; Bezae, Ψ and the Byzantine text, followed by the SBLGNT, give no number.

readings.w: P74, Sinaiticus, Alexandrinus, Ephraemi and Laudianus (reported by Metzger); NA28, THGNT, Textus Receptus (KJV "three men")
readings.orig: ἄνδρες τρεῖς ζητοῦντές σε
readings.en: three men are seeking you
readings.plain: three men are searching for you

readings.w: Codex Vaticanus (B, 300s) (reported by Metzger); Westcott-Hort
readings.orig: ἄνδρες δύο ζητοῦντές σε
readings.en: two men are seeking you
readings.plain: two men are searching for you

readings.w: SBLGNT
readings.orig: Ἰδοὺ ἄνδρες ζητοῦντές σε
readings.en: look, men seeking you
readings.plain: men are searching for you

readings.w: Codex Bezae (D, 400s), Ψ (044, 800s–900s) and most later manuscripts (reported by Metzger); Byzantine text
readings.orig: Ἰδού, ἄνδρες ζητοῦσίν σε
readings.en: look, men are seeking you
readings.plain: men are searching for you

why: The Plain follows NA28 and the Tyndale House edition here, against the SBLGNT. "Three" has the widest early support and fits 10:7 (two servants and a soldier) and 11:11. "Two" may count only the servants. Leaving the number out (in the SBLGNT with a participle, in Bezae and the Byzantine text with a plain verb) may be original, as the SBLGNT editors judged, with the numbers added from the story; or it may be a scribe's way out of the two-or-three problem.

a: So Peter went down to the men.
t: "Which were sent unto him from Cornelius"
p: The KJV adds that the men "were sent unto him from Cornelius." The words are in very few manuscripts.

readings.w: Nearly all manuscripts; NA28, SBLGNT, THGNT, Byzantine text
readings.orig: καταβὰς δὲ Πέτρος πρὸς τοὺς ἄνδρας
readings.en: Peter went down to the men
readings.plain: So Peter went down to the men.

readings.w: A few late manuscripts; Textus Receptus (KJV)
readings.orig: ... πρὸς τοὺς ἄνδρας τοὺς ἀπεσταλμένους ἀπὸ τοῦ Κορνηλίου πρὸς αὐτόν
readings.en: ... to the men who were sent from Cornelius to him
readings.plain: So Peter went down to the men Cornelius had sent to him.

why: The extra words explain who "the men" are, a typical scribal help. They are not in the Byzantine majority and came into print through the Textus Receptus.

a: he came into Caesarea
p: Editions differ on whether Peter alone or the whole group is said to arrive.

readings.w: NA28, SBLGNT, Westcott-Hort
readings.orig: εἰσῆλθεν εἰς τὴν Καισάρειαν
readings.en: he entered Caesarea
readings.plain: he came into Caesarea

readings.w: Tyndale House GNT, Byzantine text, Textus Receptus (KJV "they entered into Caesarea")
readings.orig: εἰσῆλθον εἰς τὴν Καισάρειαν
readings.en: they entered Caesarea
readings.plain: they came into Caesarea

why: The singular keeps the focus on Peter, as the verse before does, and a scribe would naturally make it plural to match "them" later in the verse. The two forms differ by one letter; either way the whole party arrived.

a: Just as Peter was going in, Cornelius came to meet him.
p: Codex Bezae tells the arrival more fully: a slave runs ahead to announce Peter, and Cornelius jumps up to meet him.

readings.w: Nearly all manuscripts; NA28, SBLGNT, THGNT, Byzantine text
readings.orig: ὡς δὲ ἐγένετο τοῦ εἰσελθεῖν τὸν Πέτρον, συναντήσας αὐτῷ ὁ Κορνήλιος
readings.en: as Peter was entering, Cornelius met him
readings.plain: Just as Peter was going in, Cornelius came to meet him.

readings.w: Codex Bezae (D, 400s) and some other Western witnesses (reported by Metzger)
readings.orig: προσεγγίζοντος δὲ τοῦ Πέτρου εἰς τὴν Καισάρειαν προδραμὼν εἷς τῶν δούλων διεσάφησεν παραγεγονέναι αὐτόν· ὁ δὲ Κορνήλιος ἐκπηδήσας καὶ συναντήσας αὐτῷ
readings.en: as Peter was approaching Caesarea, one of the slaves ran ahead and announced that he had arrived; and Cornelius jumped up and met him
readings.plain: As Peter was getting near Caesarea, one of the slaves ran ahead and announced that he had come, and Cornelius jumped up and came to meet him.

why: Bezae's reading is one of many places where the Western text of Acts adds lively detail. It smooths a real puzzle (where exactly did Cornelius meet Peter, outside or inside?), which is a sign of a later hand. It is still very old, a witness to how Acts was read in the second century.
b: The Western text of Acts, best known from Codex Bezae, is about 8.5 percent longer than the text in most Bibles. Bezae's pages for 8:29–10:14 are lost; from 10:15 on it can be heard again (see 10:19).

a: at just this hour, I was praying in my house at the ninth hour
p: The KJV says Cornelius was "fasting until this hour." The oldest copies mention only prayer.

readings.w: P74, Sinaiticus, the first hand of Alexandrinus, Vaticanus and Ephraemi (reported by Metzger); NA28, SBLGNT, THGNT
readings.orig: μέχρι ταύτης τῆς ὥρας ἤμην τὴν ἐνάτην προσευχόμενος ἐν τῷ οἴκῳ μου
readings.en: until this hour I was praying the ninth hour in my house
readings.plain: at just this hour, I was praying in my house at the ninth hour

readings.w: A corrector of Alexandrinus, Bezae (D), Laudianus (E) and most later manuscripts (reported by Metzger); Byzantine text, Textus Receptus (KJV "I was fasting until this hour; and at the ninth hour I prayed")
readings.orig: μέχρι ταύτης τῆς ὥρας ἤμην νηστεύων, καὶ τὴν ἐνάτην ὥραν προσευχόμενος ἐν τῷ οἴκῳ μου
readings.en: until this hour I was fasting, and at the ninth hour praying in my house
readings.plain: I was fasting until this very hour, and at the ninth hour I was praying in my house

why: Copyists in the early church, who prized fasting, added it in several places where prayer is mentioned (compare Mark 9:29 and 1 Corinthians 7:5). The shorter reading has the oldest support.

a: the seaside home of Simon the tanner.'
t: "When he comes, he will speak to you"
p: Most later manuscripts add that Peter "will speak to you" when he comes.

readings.w: P74, Sinaiticus, the first hand of Alexandrinus, and Vaticanus (reported by Metzger); NA28, SBLGNT, THGNT
readings.orig: ἐν οἰκίᾳ Σίμωνος βυρσέως παρὰ θάλασσαν
readings.en: in the house of Simon a tanner by the sea
readings.plain: the seaside home of Simon the tanner.'

readings.w: Ephraemi, Bezae, Laudianus and most later manuscripts (reported by Metzger); Byzantine text, Textus Receptus (KJV "who, when he cometh, shall speak unto thee")
readings.orig: ... παρὰ θάλασσαν· ὃς παραγενόμενος λαλήσει σοι
readings.en: ... by the sea; who, when he comes, will speak to you
readings.plain: the seaside home of Simon the tanner. When he comes, he will speak to you.'

why: The clause rounds off the angel's message and prepares for 10:33; it was easy to add, and the oldest copies lack it.

a: all the Lord has given you orders to say
p: The later text and the KJV say "commanded thee of God."

readings.w: The oldest manuscripts; NA28, SBLGNT, THGNT
readings.orig: τὰ προστεταγμένα σοι ὑπὸ τοῦ κυρίου
readings.en: the things commanded you by the Lord
readings.plain: all the Lord has given you orders to say

readings.w: Byzantine text, Textus Receptus (KJV "all things that are commanded thee of God")
readings.orig: τὰ προστεταγμένα σοι ὑπὸ τοῦ θεοῦ
readings.en: the things commanded you by God
readings.plain: all God has given you orders to say

why: "God" was probably brought in from "before God" earlier in the same sentence. The meaning hardly changes.

a: in the name of Jesus Christ
p: The older text says Peter had them baptized "in the name of Jesus Christ"; the later text and the KJV say "of the Lord."

readings.w: The oldest manuscripts; NA28, SBLGNT, THGNT
readings.orig: ἐν τῷ ὀνόματι Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ βαπτισθῆναι
readings.en: to be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ
readings.plain: in the name of Jesus Christ

readings.w: Byzantine text, Textus Receptus (KJV "in the name of the Lord")
readings.orig: βαπτισθῆναι ἐν τῷ ὀνόματι τοῦ κυρίου
readings.en: to be baptized in the name of the Lord
readings.plain: in the name of the Lord

why: "Jesus Christ" has the older support and matches 2:38. On whether "in the name of" means a spoken formula, see the note on 8:16 and the card at 2:38.
